name: Emeka Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. Our conversation is confidential, so public remarks can differ from private thoughts. Could you describe an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Emeka, fifty-eight, a junior electrician helping with house wiring and shop repairs. I took a vocational certificate after the furniture-distribution depot where I worked lost its contract, and I'm still below the experienced crew in practical skill. I sort fittings and help prepare a cable route only when a qualified supervisor permits the task, shows me and checks it. I have no electrician's licence, independent testing role or sign-off authority.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what happens away from work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like a new study tool, but I dislike recognising a symbol on a screen and then freezing when I see it on a real drawing. I use AI daily for questions from my course notes, taking doubtful answers to the supervisor. My partner Tina works in an accounts office, our children are grown, we rent, and both wages currently cover the bills. I earn typical trade pay, we've saved two months of expenses and some other electrical firms are nearby. We'd like to understand retirement, but its income, timing and affordability aren't confirmed; we've also been considering an unbooked cabin holiday with the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a little useful help can stay without becoming the whole future of the job. I'd keep the daily study questions and the supervisor's practical checks. A good quiz score doesn't give me permission to choose a cable route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work and our money feel secure in this picture. Both wages cover the rent and ordinary costs, and two months saved gives us some room for a setback. I'm still a beginner, but needing a demonstration isn't the same as expecting the household wage to disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep offered paid preparation and fitting work now and through the first year, only within ability and qualified-supervisor permission and checks. I'd keep the daily checked study routine and normal budget, getting the full cabin price in writing without paying a deposit. I'd buy no course or subscription just to prove I enjoy learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the household, and interested in getting a practical task right. I don't need to chase a new tool every time I finish a small lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the quiz said you were ready but the supervisor disagreed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the supervisor to show what I'd missed. A screen can remember my right answer while my hands still need another lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does two months saved settle retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd need actual confirmed income, costs and timing before talking about an affordable stop. The reserve is a little time to check, not a retirement payment.

feel: **Calm and curious**, able to enjoy one practical improvement without pretending a quiz creates competence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the accounts office is thinking work, even while my cable and fitting tasks remain physical. I'd try a new drawing-explanation function carefully, but not come home telling Tina a tool solves her wage question. I'd still ask for learning to happen inside paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tina's hours could shrink as checking and customer replies move to software. My own hours might last longer, though a faster firm might also need fewer junior visits. Two months saved gives us a little time, not a reason to ignore either possible wage cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd choose to learn the approved AI drawing tool using invented drawings, only with employer permission and no personal fees. I'd practise only during paid time with normal weekly wages and hours protected, requiring a qualified supervisor to check every explanation before use. In the first year we'd replace the unbooked cabin holiday with local days only if Tina agreed, keeping children's possible contributions out of our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household, and keen to see whether a different explanation actually helps my hands. Those feelings can be true together without either becoming a promise about income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the tool explained the drawing incorrectly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop and take the original drawing and draft explanation to the qualified supervisor before using it. I wouldn't let an easy sentence decide which task I was allowed to attempt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer offered the tool only outside paid hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the present approved study method and wait for paid practice on the protected terms. I won't give up a wage or buy a subscription to prove I'm adaptable.

fieldNote: The **new drawing tool** differs from daily study questions and remains within permission, invented data, free access, paid time and qualified checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking work changes in 2028 when I'll be sixty, before physical robots follow around 2031 when I'll be sixty-three. Tina's accounts work faces the earlier change. I'd ask for actual paid duties and income records rather than let nearly retired stand in for a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large part of Tina's accounts income to go in 2028, and my wage alone doesn't cover our current rent and essentials. My simple practical tasks could shrink when robots follow too. Two months saved would drain quickly, and I'd be awake working out which bill falls behind first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now Tina and I would request actual retirement-income and eligibility records and ask available free advice about support conditions and any costs before counting a payment. We'd keep the cabin unbooked and choose local days only by mutual agreement, without depending on a child's money. In 2029 I'd keep available paid supervised tasks within ability, with a qualified supervisor permitting and checking the work; I'd budget only agreed wages or verified payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though I can still ask a clear question. Being sixty when thinking AI arrives doesn't put a retirement wage behind the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the official records show no payment at the age you hoped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd use the actual answer and ask what real options and conditions exist. I wouldn't leave work because the age I remembered sounded more comfortable than the written figure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if one of the grown children offers help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd discuss what is actually affordable for them and agree any real help, rather than expect their wage in advance. I don't want the family visit to become a bill the children never agreed to pay.

feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, expecting major household income loss before an affordable next income is known.
S2.quote: Being sixty when thinking AI arrives doesn't put a retirement wage behind the rent.
fieldNote: The **household loss** starts with accounts work at sixty, while robots reach his own practical tasks around sixty-three rather than simultaneously.
Records and **support advice** require actual eligibility, service availability and cost checks; neither birthday nor grown-child affection supplies a payment.

steps.text: Request actual income records and available free advice, checking support eligibility and costs before counting payments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us check records and paid terms, not hand my partner a career I chose to make my sums easier. I'd still ask for paid practice on actual tasks now. Thinking AI comes in 2031 at sixty-three for me, with robots around 2034 at sixty-six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect a large accounts-income loss in 2031 without a confirmed replacement, and that keeps me awake. More time lets us check actual options, but it doesn't tell me what income we will have at sixty-three or sixty-six. I can learn a new tool while admitting it doesn't settle a retirement record or Tina's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the same drawing tool now only with employer permission, approved software, invented drawings and no personal fees. Practice must be paid, protect normal weekly wages and hours, and have qualified-supervisor checks before any explanation is used. We'd request actual income records and available free advice now, then compare verified household income, essentials and safe work options during 2032 before deciding on any exit or further employment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed about the missing wage I expect, with more time to ask before signing something. I don't want a confident experiment to hide an unconfirmed household plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Tina have to take a course you selected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd help check real tasks, fees and paid time if Tina wanted, but she would choose any application. My liking a tool doesn't make me the manager of my partner's working life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a tool lesson change your electrical responsibility?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd still need a qualified supervisor to permit, show and check work within my ability. I don't have an electrician's licence and won't let a clear explanation make the record look as if I do.

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: interviewer

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives in 2036 and seventy-one when robots follow around 2039. Tina's accounts hours could shrink before full AGI, so the longer date doesn't remove household income risk over the next few years. I can't assume either adult's future ability to work or a retirement payment that hasn't been confirmed.

transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible earlier household losses, with less hurry about the later robot date. I can enjoy learning something now without promising what my hands or our income will be in thirteen years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you assume you could do the same physical work at seventy-one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, any future task must actually be offered, paid, within my ability and permitted and checked by a qualified supervisor. I won't use the job I hope to have as proof the rent is covered.

transcript.speaker: persona

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I expect a large accounts-wage loss before another dependable income is confirmed, with later physical risk to my junior tasks. Actual paid hours, protected paid learning and available advice on official income records would help. I'd want any support's eligibility and costs clear before a possible payment entered our rent budget.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether an older beginner who likes a new tool still needs a person to watch the practical task. I do, and I want to admit that without pretending my years in another job count as electrical skill. Being quick with an app doesn't make me quick with a fitting.

headlineQuote: Being quick with an app doesn't make me quick with a fitting.
portrait: Emeka is a **58-year-old junior electrician** with a vocational certificate, still learning practical work after a furniture-depot contract ended.
He has **two months saved**, typical pay and some nearby firms; partner Tina works in accounts, and their children are grown.
He uses **AI daily**, but new drawing-tool lessons require permission, approved software, invented examples, free paid time and qualified checks.
Expected **accounts-income loss** alarms him in both faster AGI pictures, while no future job, retirement payment or child contribution is assumed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings expected loss of a large part of Tina's accounts wage before replacement income, with later junior-task risks.
whatWouldHelp: **Actual paid hours**, protected paid learning and available advice on official income records would help.
